mcqs.question: Which single change distinguishes uniform convergence from pointwise convergence in the ε–N definition?

options.A: Uniform convergence requires ε to be smaller
options.B: N depends only on ε, not on x, in uniform convergence
options.C: Uniform convergence only applies to continuous functions
options.D: Pointwise convergence requires the domain to be bounded

mcqs.explanation: The entire distinction is that in uniform convergence, one N works simultaneously for every x in the domain.

whyOthersWrong.A: ε plays the same role in both definitions.
whyOthersWrong.C: Both pointwise and uniform convergence can apply to any functions, continuous or not.
whyOthersWrong.D: Neither definition requires a bounded domain.

mcqs.question: Which sequence is the standard textbook counterexample showing pointwise convergence does not preserve continuity?
mcqs.explanation: f_n(x)=x^n converges pointwise to a function that jumps from 0 to 1 at x=1, despite every f_n being continuous.

whyOthersWrong.A: This converges uniformly to 0 — no discontinuity issue.
whyOthersWrong.C: This converges uniformly to 0 by a direct supremum bound.
whyOthersWrong.D: This converges pointwise to a continuous limit (0); the failure here is with integration, not continuity.

mcqs.question: Which of the following fails to be a metric on R?
mcqs.explanation: d(x,y)=(x-y)^2 fails the triangle inequality — e.g. with x=0,y=1,z=2, d(x,z)=4 but d(x,y)+d(y,z)=2.

whyOthersWrong.B: A well-known bounded metric equivalent to the standard one.
whyOthersWrong.D: Also a valid bounded metric equivalent to the standard one.

mcqs.question: Which statement about completeness is correct?

options.A: Every bounded metric space is complete
options.B: (0,1) with the usual metric is complete
options.C: Q with the usual metric is not complete

mcqs.explanation: Q is not complete: rational truncations of √2 form a Cauchy sequence with no rational limit.

whyOthersWrong.A: Boundedness has nothing to do with completeness — (0,1) is bounded but incomplete.
whyOthersWrong.B: (0,1) is a standard example of an incomplete space (the Cauchy sequence 1/n has no limit in (0,1)).
whyOthersWrong.D: Completeness only requires Cauchy sequences to converge, not every sequence.

mcqs.question: A contraction mapping T on a metric space X with contraction constant k<1 fails to have a fixed point in X. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The contraction constant must actually be greater than 1

mcqs.explanation: The Banach Fixed-Point Theorem requires X to be complete; on an incomplete space, a genuine contraction can have no fixed point (e.g. T(x)=x/2 on (0,1]).

whyOthersWrong.A: The premise already states k<1, a genuine contraction.
whyOthersWrong.C: Every contraction is automatically continuous (even Lipschitz).
whyOthersWrong.D: Contractions on complete spaces always have a unique fixed point — that's the whole theorem.
